Posted May 23, 2004
Analysis by Richard Cowan Sponsored by Advanced Nutrients.

George Bush supposedly thinks that God wanted him to be President. That should have the rest of us asking why God would want to punish us so terribly. We might find a clue in a saying from the ancient world: Whom the gods would destroy, first they make mad.

Madness is the inability to perceive reality and/or think clearly about it. That seems to be a pretty good description of the Bush Administration and the processes that led to it.

However, this madness is not of a clinical nature, and neither is it of divine origin, but rather comes from a lack of honesty and failure of critical thinking skills. Of course, this is much more widespread than actual mental illness.

We can see this in recent news items:

PARENTS DRIVE KIDS TO DRINK said the headline on one story about a report by Statistics Canada that noted, If interactions with parents were characterized by nagging, inconsistent enforcement of rules, threats and anger, the odds of the adolescent getting drunk and using drugs were relatively high.

There were similar stories in most of the Canadian media even though the same paragraph in the StatsCan report warned, Still, it cannot be inferred that hostile parenting causes substance use. It is possible that the parents' way of dealing with the adolescent may have changed in response to behavioral problems such as alcohol or drug use.

In other words, the kids may be driven to drink by the parents or the parents may be driven to nag by the kids using alcohol and other drugs. The point recognized here is that correlation is not causality. That is the fundamental error in the so-called gateway theory and much prohibitionist propaganda.
See
Columbia University Prostitutes Itself. JAMA Publishes Racist Claptrap. The Lancet Upholds Its Standards.

To its vast credit, Statscan does not even mention the gateway, but that may be because the report shows that marijuana is not the first drug used by kids.

The average age at which adolescents reported having their first drink was 12.4 years, with only a slight difference between boys and girls. The average age of being drunk for the first time was about a year older, at just past 13 years.

Glue-sniffing began at an average age of just over 12 years. For other drugs, including marijuana and hallucinogens, the average age of first-time use was older, between 13.1 and 13.8.

The StatsCan report highlighted other examples in which cause and effect are not clear.

The study adds to evidence that peer behaviour is related to an adolescent's own alcohol and drug use. However, it is not possible to determine a causal direction. For example, friendships may provide opportunities to learn through imitation and reinforce behaviour. It could also be that " birds of a feather flock together, " and adolescents seek friends with similar attitudes toward alcohol and other drugs.

Statscan does not note that in all of these situations it is also possible that there were actually some other difficulties that caused both the problematic parental behavior and the problematic substance use.

For example, perhaps the nagging parents were unhappy because of poverty or illness, and the kids were also stressed by these problems and self-medicated. Or perhaps they were both the victims of prohibitionist propaganda which encourages parents to lie to their children as often as possible about marijuana.
(They may have been following the advice given on Tips for Parents What To Do and When)

The need for critical thinking also applies to the debate over the value of anecdotal evidence.

It has been said that the plural of anecdote is data. However, some anecdotes are more equal than others.
From 1997 see
British Medical Association Runs A Non-Debate On Medical Marijuana
The Prohibitionist Ignores the Fact That Patients Are Being Arrested
 Unless Court Records Are Just Anecdotal Evidence.

If thousands of people with AIDS, MS, cancer, etc., report that cannabis alleviates their suffering, this is dismissed as anecdotal evidence and we cannot stop arresting sick people just because they claim that they feel better.

On the other hand, if someone reports that a problem followed cannabis use, cannabis is blamed for that problem, and we cannot stop arresting healthy people who are not having problems, because someday they might.

Although the StatsCan report did not deal with mental illness, the points that they raised about causality are also applicable to the correlation between cannabis use and schizophrenia.

Does cannabis use cause, precipitate and/or aggravate schizophrenia? Or do people with schizophrenia self-medicate with cannabis? In that case it would be schizophrenia causing cannabis use. Or does prohibition aggravate all mental health problems?
See
Classic Reefer Madness At London Times: " Woman who killed father 'driven mad by cannabis.' " Quacks and Hacks and Schizophrenia. Is It Paranoid to Distrust Politicized Science?
and
 " Young men who take cannabis are five times more likely to be violent than those who avoid the drug. " No, But I Am At Least Five Times More Likely to Be Violent When I Read This Sort Of Crap.
and
 " Cannabis May Help Combat Schizophrenia "
Or " Marijuana-Like Chemical Found In Schizophrenics "
 Is Schizophrenia A Journalistic Disorder? -- 2 Articles

When someone who has used cannabis is diagnosed with mental illness, cannabis is assumed to be at least a contributing cause. However, when people with mental illness report that cannabis helps cope with their problems, that is ignored or dismissed. After all, they are crazy, aren't they?

Of course, neither side of the argument wants to consider that both may be right. I have had a number of people tell me that cannabis has greatly alleviated their problems with mental illness, but it is at least possible that improper dosing with cannabis could aggravate mental problems. One of the adverse consequences of the deinstitutionalization of the mentally ill is that it is often very difficult for them to self-medicate properly even with measured doses of a prescription drug.

It is vastly more difficult for impoverished and marginalized people with mental problems to obtain cannabis in a way that would allow for its proper use to deal with their condition. Even in Holland, where cannabis is easily accessible in relatively predictable and consistent dosages, persons with mental illness will have difficulty knowing how to use cannabis properly. It would be difficult for an individual doctor to know how to prescribe proper dosages.

However, ignorance does not stop Canadian doctors from opposing the legalization of cannabis, medical or otherwise. Indeed, their self-proclaimed ignorance is not an occasion for modesty, but rather a further arrogation of power.
See
Cruelty, Incompetence, And Quackery Threaten Canadian Medical Cannabis Patients.

Often there is a circular process at work in which doctors are encouraged by laymen who have been mislead by other doctors.
See
Health Canada's Office of Cannabis Medical Access' Stakeholder Advisory Committee Includes Physicians for A Smoke Free Canada - Not The Compassion Societies. But It Will Let Them Talk For An Hour

Yesterday, Saskatchewan papers reported that the Schizophrenia Society of Saskatchewan was urging the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Saskatchewan to have its members to be sure their patients do not have a history of schizophrenia prior to prescribing medical marijuana.
The full text of the article is online at http://www.freedomtoexhale.com/warn.htm

Here are a few excerpts:

Members of our society reported that their ill relatives have been hinting at their interest to seek out medical specialists in an effort to have marijuana prescribed for their chronic pain.

Since many of these consumers can be very persuasive and manipulative, we felt that we should make you and your members aware in the event that some of these persons whose medical history is unknown to your members come shopping around for such prescriptions. "

It went on to say that many people with schizophrenia are addicted to drugs or alcohol as a way to cope with their illness.

But here is the best part:

Finding a doctor to prescribe marijuana would justify their smoking it and they would have one less thing to worry about because they couldn't be charged with possessing the drug.

The Society's warning found a receptive audience. The article reports that the College of Physicians and Surgeons included an excerpt from the society's letter in one of its newsletters sent to doctors throughout Saskatchewan.

Dr. Karen Shaw, deputy registrar of the College says people with schizophrenia aren't the only ones who may be looking for a prescription for marijuana.

" There is a population out there that is going to find something to try and get access to medical marijuana which will decrease the problem they have accessing it and the risk of a criminal record, " she said.

Shaw acknowledged, " Sometimes it's not easy to diagnose chronic pain conditions.

The college expects doctors to use medical marijuana as a last resort after all other options have been tried and found to be ineffective.

Shaw says the lack of research and medical trials of medical marijuana is troubling, and doctors don't fully understand what the long-term implications are of taking medical marijuana.

Now let's get this straight, so to speak.

Both the Schizophrenia Society and College of Physicians and Surgeons recognize that chronic pain is hard to treat, and they admit that they do not know much about cannabis, and they recognize that the patients are in danger of being arrested when they have to go to the black market, where they get cannabis of uncertain levels of cannabinoids.

Nonetheless, they think that this is preferable to having them get it from a legal source.

Consider that the Society's website says, The role of stress is unclear; however, it is acknowledged that stress can trigger or worsen symptoms when the illness is already present. Stress is very individual but could be accompanied with an exam, a move, a loss of someone, a difficult relationship, use of street drugs etc.
From http://www.schizophrenia.sk.ca/causes.htm

The use of street drugs, etc can cause stress. Could part of that stress be from a fear of the police?

After all, the Society also recognizes that There may be the false belief of being persecuted.
From http://www.schizophrenia.sk.ca/symptoms.htm

But what if there were a conspiracy by the Schizophrenia Society and College of Physicians and Surgeons, their friends, to deprive them of something to relieve their chronic pain or other problems and to keep them at risk of arrest.

You would have to be paranoid to believe that!

Contrast this perversity with the view expressed last week in The Lancet:

" Despite widespread concern, we have found no strong evidence that use of cannabis in itself has important consequences for psychological or social health. This finding is not equivalent to the conclusion that use of cannabis is harmless in psychosocial terms; problems with the available evidence render it equally unable to support this proposition. Better evidence is needed in relation to cannabis, which is widely used, and in relation to other drugs that, although less widely used, might have important effects ".

In an accompanying Commentary (p 1568) Franjo Grotenhermen from the Nova-Institut GmbH, Germany, states: " There is some reason to believe that cannabis contributes to psychosocial problems in adolescents and young adults, and no responsible adult would want young people to take drugs. There is no question that this issue is an important candidate for education and prevention, but there is a fierce debate on the place repressive measures should have in this context. There is little reason to believe that criminalisation has had a strong effect on the extent of cannabis use by young people. Moreover, prohibition itself seems to increase the harmfulness of drug use and cause social harm.
See
Columbia University Prostitutes Itself. JAMA Publishes Racist Claptrap. The Lancet Upholds Its Standards.

There is one consistent theme that runs throughout all these situations.

Prohibition does not prevent cannabis use by children or the mentally ill, the vulnerable populations whom we supposedly want to protect. Instead, cannabis prohibition makes it more difficult for parents, patients, society, and doctors to control cannabis use.

The Drug War makes honest education about cannabis impossible, and leaves cannabis users marginalized in ways that make their lives more stressful. This stress is unhealthy for everyone, but it is certainly most damaging to people with schizophrenia.

Cannabis prohibition is not merely a failure; it is a counterproductive fraud that is harming those whom we claim we want to protect.
